quiz.q: A man is bitten on the hand by his cat two hours ago. There are two small punctures over the back of the hand with minimal bleeding. What is the correct management?
choices: Irrigate and close the punctures with 5-0 nylon
Irrigate, leave open, start amoxicillin-clavulanate, address tetanus, and arrange a 48-hour recheck
Irrigate and discharge with cephalexin
Reassure; puncture wounds this small do not become infected
quiz.why: Cat bites infect in 30 to 50% of cases and hand bites are higher risk still, so they are left open with prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate. Cephalexin does not cover Pasteurella, and closing the puncture seals the inoculum inside.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old has a 6 mm laceration over his fourth knuckle. He says he punched a wall. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: A simple laceration suitable for adhesive closure
A boxer's fracture wound that can be closed after x-ray
A clenched-fist injury — assume joint penetration, x-ray for a tooth fragment, hand surgery, do not close
A contusion requiring only ice and elevation
quiz.why: A wound over a knuckle from a punch is a fight bite until proven otherwise, and the tooth enters the joint with the fist closed. Closing it traps oral anaerobes and Eikenella inside a joint, which destroys it.

quiz.q: A patient lacerated his forearm on a window. He insists something is still in there, but the wound looks clean. What should be done?
choices: Obtain a plain radiograph, since glass is radiopaque and the sensation predicts a retained fragment
Close the wound; a clean-appearing wound excludes foreign body
Obtain an ultrasound instead, since glass does not appear on plain film
Explore blindly with forceps
quiz.why: Glass fragments over about 2 mm are usually visible on plain film, and a patient's sensation of a foreign body is a genuinely predictive symptom. Blind probing pushes fragments deeper, and ultrasound is reserved for radiolucent material.

quiz.q: A patient has a laceration at the base of the little finger. She can move the finger fully but cannot spread her fingers apart. Which structure is injured?
choices: Median nerve
Radial nerve
Ulnar nerve
Flexor digitorum profundus
quiz.why: Finger abduction and adduction are ulnar motor functions. The median nerve controls thumb opposition, the radial nerve controls wrist and finger extension, and an FDP injury would prevent fingertip flexion rather than spreading.

quiz.q: A finger laceration is bleeding steadily from one edge. What is the correct control measure?
choices: Clamp the vessel with a hemostat
Apply a tourniquet at the wrist for 30 minutes
Direct pressure and elevation
Inject lidocaine with epinephrine into the bleeding point
quiz.why: Digital nerves run alongside digital arteries, so clamping takes the nerve with the vessel. Pressure and elevation control any bleeding a hand can produce, and a wrist tourniquet is neither necessary nor benign.

quiz.q: Which wound should be left open for delayed closure?
choices: A clean 4 cm facial laceration presenting at hour 9
A puncture wound of the sole from a nail presenting at hour 1
A scalp laceration presenting at hour 6
A clean forearm incision presenting at hour 3
quiz.why: Punctures cannot be irrigated effectively and are never closed primarily. Face and scalp are richly vascular and are closed well beyond the classic window, and a clean fresh incision is an ideal primary closure.

quiz.q: A 60 kg patient requires local anesthesia with 1% lidocaine with epinephrine. What is the maximum volume?
choices: 27 mL
42 mL
50 mL
14 mL
quiz.why: 7 mg/kg x 60 kg = 420 mg, and 1% is 10 mg/mL, so 42 mL. 27 mL corresponds to the plain lidocaine limit of 4.5 mg/kg, and 50 mL exceeds the ceiling.

quiz.q: A 4 cm laceration needs irrigation. What volume and pressure are appropriate?
choices: About 200 to 400 mL at 5 to 8 psi using a splash shield on a 30 to 60 mL syringe
About 50 mL poured from a saline bottle
About 1 L of povidone-iodine solution
About 100 mL of hydrogen peroxide
quiz.why: Roughly 50 to 100 mL per centimeter at 5 to 8 psi is the standard. Pouring produces no mechanical cleaning, and iodine and peroxide are toxic to fibroblasts and never go inside a wound.

quiz.q: A child has a 2 cm linear forehead laceration with edges that meet on their own. Which approach is best?
choices: Staples after LET application
Adhesive strips without any anesthesia
Injected lidocaine and 4-0 nylon
Topical LET followed by tissue adhesive
quiz.why: A short, clean, low-tension facial wound with apposed edges is the ideal adhesive candidate, and LET avoids a needle in a child. Staples are not used on the face, and 4-0 nylon is far too heavy for facial skin.

quiz.q: A patient returns 3 days after a repair with worsening pain, spreading redness and a streak tracking toward the elbow. What does the streak represent?
choices: Lymphangitis, indicating spreading infection
A normal healing response
Venous thrombosis
An allergic reaction to the suture material
quiz.why: A red streak tracking proximally toward the nodes is lymphangitis and signals a spreading infection needing systemic treatment. Normal healing does not track, and a suture allergy produces local itching rather than a linear streak.

quiz.q: A patient describes a painful, swollen "spider bite" on the thigh that he never saw bite him. It is fluctuant. What is most likely and what is the treatment?
choices: A true arachnid envenomation requiring antivenom
A sebaceous cyst requiring elective excision
Cellulitis requiring cephalexin alone
A MRSA abscess requiring incision and drainage
quiz.why: An unwitnessed "spider bite" that is fluctuant is a MRSA abscess in the overwhelming majority of cases, and drainage is the treatment. Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate a walled-off collection.

quiz.q: A patient with a heavily soiled farm injury has never been vaccinated against tetanus. What is required?
choices: Tetanus vaccine alone
Tetanus immune globulin alone
Tetanus vaccine plus tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM
Neither, if the wound is thoroughly irrigated
quiz.why: Fewer than three lifetime doses plus a non-clean wound requires both active vaccine and passive immune globulin, because the vaccine takes weeks to protect. Irrigation reduces bacterial load but does not neutralize toxin.

quiz.q: A child is bitten by a neighbour's healthy, vaccinated dog that is available for observation. What is the rabies management?
choices: Begin immune globulin and the full vaccine series now
Observe the dog for 10 days; no prophylaxis unless it becomes ill
Give vaccine on days 0 and 3 only
Euthanize and test the dog immediately
quiz.why: A healthy, available dog, cat or ferret is observed for 10 days, and prophylaxis begins only if it develops signs. Immediate full prophylaxis is reserved for bats and wild carnivores or an unavailable animal.

quiz.q: Which burn depth counts toward the TBSA used for fluid calculations?
choices: All burns including superficial
Partial-thickness and full-thickness only
Full-thickness only
Only burns over a major joint
quiz.why: Superficial burns do not leak the plasma that drives resuscitation volume, so they are excluded. Counting them inflates the calculated volume substantially and over-resuscitates the patient.

quiz.q: A patient arrives 20 minutes after scalding her forearm. What is the correct immediate care?
choices: Apply ice packs for 20 minutes
Cool running water for 20 minutes, then clean and dress
Apply silver sulfadiazine immediately without cooling
Rupture all blisters before dressing
quiz.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes is effective up to 3 hours after the burn. Ice causes further tissue injury, and small intact blisters are generally left alone rather than routinely ruptured.

quiz.q: A patient has a circumferential full-thickness burn of the forearm. Doppler signals in the fingers are fading. What is needed?
choices: Fasciotomy
Additional fluid resuscitation only
Elevation and observation
Escharotomy through the burned skin
quiz.why: Rigid eschar acts as a tourniquet as the limb swells beneath it, and the fix is an incision through the dead skin. A fasciotomy cuts deeper and treats compartment syndrome, and observation loses the hand.

quiz.q: Which burn does NOT by itself meet burn center referral criteria?
choices: A partial-thickness burn of the palm
An electrical burn from a 240 V source
A 4% superficial sunburn of the back
A 2% full-thickness burn of the forearm
quiz.why: Superficial burns are not referral criteria regardless of area. Hands, all electrical burns and any full-thickness burn all qualify on their own.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old fell on an outstretched hand. The elbow x-ray shows no fracture line but there is a posterior fat pad. How is this interpreted?
choices: A normal finding in children
Always abnormal — it indicates an effusion and an occult fracture, likely supracondylar
Evidence of a chronic elbow problem
An artifact of positioning
quiz.why: A posterior fat pad is never normal; it is displaced by a joint effusion, which in this setting means an occult supracondylar fracture. Treating it as normal sends home a fracture that threatens the brachial artery.

quiz.q: A patient with a humeral shaft fracture cannot extend the wrist and has numbness in the first dorsal web space. Which nerve is injured?
choices: Median
Ulnar
Axillary
Radial
quiz.why: The radial nerve runs in a groove along the back of the humerus and is injured in 10 to 18% of shaft fractures, producing wrist drop and first web space numbness. The median and ulnar nerves supply the hand differently, and the axillary nerve supplies the deltoid.

quiz.q: A patient with anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall has a normal wrist series. What should happen?
choices: Discharge with an elastic wrap and analgesia
Thumb spica splint and repeat imaging or MRI in 10 to 14 days
Repeat the x-ray in 24 hours
Immediate CT of the wrist for every case
quiz.why: Scaphoid fractures are frequently invisible initially, and a missed one risks avascular necrosis from the retrograde blood supply. A wrap provides no protection, and 24 hours is too early for a fracture line to appear.

quiz.q: Which injury pairs a fracture with a dislocation at the other end of the forearm?
choices: Colles fracture
Boxer's fracture
Monteggia fracture-dislocation
Barton fracture
quiz.why: Monteggia is a proximal ulna fracture with a dislocated radial head, which is why the joint above and below is always imaged. A Colles and a Barton are both distal radius patterns, and a boxer's fracture involves the fifth metacarpal.

quiz.q: A patient has a mallet finger. What is the correct treatment?
choices: Buddy taping for 2 weeks
Continuous extension splinting of the distal joint for 6 to 8 weeks, never allowing it to bend
Immediate surgical repair in all cases
Range of motion exercises beginning at 48 hours
quiz.why: The avulsed extensor must be held in continuous extension while it heals, and a single episode of flexion during a splint change undoes weeks of healing. Buddy taping does not control the fingertip joint, and early motion guarantees failure.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old fell at home. Her right leg is shortened and externally rotated and she cannot lift her heel off the bed. The hip x-ray is read as normal. What is the next step?
choices: Discharge with analgesia and a walker
Repeat plain films in one week
CT or MRI of the hip, because occult hip fractures are common with this exam
Physical therapy referral
quiz.why: The exam is classic for a hip fracture, and occult fractures with normal plain films are well described in this population. Discharging a patient who cannot bear weight is how a non-displaced fracture becomes a displaced one.

quiz.q: A patient with an isolated mid-shaft femur fracture also has an ipsilateral ankle fracture. Should a traction splint be used?
choices: Yes, traction splints are indicated for all femur fractures
No, because traction splints are contraindicated in all adults
Yes, but only at reduced tension
No — an ankle or foot injury on the same side is a contraindication
quiz.why: Traction splints pull against the ankle and foot, so an injury there is a contraindication, along with pelvic fractures and hip or knee injury on that side. They remain standard for genuinely isolated mid-shaft fractures.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old inverted his ankle. He has tenderness only over the anterior talofibular ligament, none over either malleolus, and he limped four steps in the department. What do the Ottawa rules recommend?
choices: Ankle and foot radiographs
Ankle radiograph only
No radiograph is required
Radiograph only if the pain persists past 48 hours
quiz.why: Neither malleolar bone tenderness nor an inability to bear weight four steps is present, so no imaging is indicated. Tenderness over a ligament is exactly the finding the rules are designed to let you skip imaging for.

quiz.q: A patient jumped from a second-storey window and has bilateral heel pain. What additional injury must be excluded?
choices: A lumbar spine fracture
A clavicle fracture
A distal radius fracture
A femoral neck fracture only
quiz.why: Axial load from landing on the heels transmits up the skeleton, and about 10% of calcaneal fractures have an associated lumbar burst fracture. Heel pain dominates the patient's attention, so the back must be asked about deliberately.

quiz.q: A footballer has severe midfoot pain, bruising across the sole of the foot, and cannot bear weight. Standard films are read as normal. What should be suspected?
choices: A simple midfoot sprain
A stress fracture of the second metatarsal only
Plantar fasciitis
A Lisfranc injury requiring weight-bearing views and orthopedic referral
quiz.why: Plantar bruising with disproportionate midfoot pain is the classic Lisfranc presentation, and non-weight-bearing films frequently look normal because the displacement only appears under load. Missing it leads to permanent midfoot arthritis.

quiz.q: Which statement about ankle sprain grading is correct?
choices: Grade III sprains are always the most painful
Grade II sprains show gross instability
Grade III sprains are complete tears and may be less painful than grade II
Grade I sprains require six weeks of casting
quiz.why: A completely torn ligament has no intact fibres left to hurt, so pain is a poor guide to severity and stability must be tested. Grade II has laxity with a firm endpoint, and grade I is treated with early protected movement.

quiz.q: A patient arrives with a deformed tibia and a 4 mm puncture wound over it. What is the most time-critical intervention?
choices: Reduction of the deformity
Antibiotics within one hour of arrival
Bedside irrigation with 3 L of saline
A CT scan of the tibia
quiz.why: Antibiotics within the hour is the intervention most strongly associated with reduced infection in open fractures. Deep irrigation belongs in the operating room, and imaging and reduction can follow the antibiotic.

quiz.q: Four hours after a tibial fracture, a casted patient has escalating pain, screams on passive toe extension, and has a strong dorsalis pedis pulse with pink toes. What is the correct action?
choices: Reassure and increase analgesia; the pulse excludes compartment syndrome
Elevate the limb above the heart and recheck in an hour
Split the cast and padding to skin, keep the limb at heart level, and escalate immediately for possible fasciotomy
Apply ice over the cast and reassess
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion plus pain on passive stretch is compartment syndrome; pulses persist because compartment pressure exceeds capillary rather than arterial pressure. Elevation reduces the perfusion gradient and analgesia only masks the sign.

quiz.q: How long after the onset of compartment syndrome does irreversible muscle necrosis begin?
choices: 4 to 6 hours
12 to 24 hours
30 minutes
48 hours
quiz.why: Muscle death begins at 4 to 6 hours, which is the entire reason this is a surgical emergency rather than a next-morning problem. Waiting 12 hours guarantees permanent contracture or amputation.

quiz.q: A patient arrives with an ankle fracture-dislocation. The skin over the medial malleolus is stretched white and the foot is dusky. What comes first?
choices: X-ray before any manipulation
Immediate reduction, before imaging
Ice and elevation while awaiting the radiology technician
Orthopedic consultation before touching the limb
quiz.why: Skin under that tension becomes necrotic within about an hour and the foot is ischemic, so reduction precedes imaging. Waiting for films or consultation costs the skin and possibly the foot.

quiz.q: You are assisting with a shoulder reduction. What is the most commonly skipped step that later matters most?
choices: Applying the sling correctly
Documenting the axillary nerve exam before the reduction
Obtaining consent for sedation
Recording the time of the reduction
quiz.why: Without a pre-reduction nerve exam nobody can tell whether a post-reduction deficit came from the injury or the procedure. The other steps matter but none of them becomes unanswerable afterwards.

quiz.q: Which crutch instruction is correct?
choices: Rest your weight on the underarm pads
Keep the pads snug against the armpits
Keep 2 to 3 finger widths between the pad and the armpit and bear weight through the hands
Lead with the injured leg going up stairs
quiz.why: Weight through the axilla compresses the radial nerve and causes crutch palsy, so the gap and hand weight-bearing are essential. On stairs the rule is up with the good leg and down with the bad.

quiz.q: A 3-month-old has a transverse femur fracture attributed to a fall from a bouncer seat. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Treat the fracture and discharge with pediatric follow-up
Report only if a second injury is found on the skeletal survey
Order vitamin D levels and defer any reporting
Recognize a fracture in a non-ambulatory infant as an abuse red flag, obtain a skeletal survey, and report the concern
quiz.why: Any fracture in an infant who cannot yet walk is a major red flag, and mandated reporting requires only reasonable cause, not proof. Deferring the report until more evidence appears defeats the purpose of mandatory reporting.

quiz.q: Which Salter-Harris type has the worst prognosis for future growth?
choices: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type V
quiz.why: Type V is a crush of the growth plate itself, frequently recognized only in hindsight once growth has already arrested. Type II is the most common and generally does well, and types I and III have better outcomes than a crush.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old will not use her arm after being swung by the hands. She holds it at her side, slightly flexed and pronated, with no swelling. What is the best next step?
choices: Reduce by hyperpronation or supination and flexion; no x-ray is needed with this history
Obtain a full x-ray series of the arm before touching it
Apply a sling and refer to orthopedics in a week
Obtain a skeletal survey
quiz.why: This is a classic nursemaid's elbow, and with a typical mechanism and no swelling or deformity imaging is unnecessary before a reduction attempt. The child uses the arm within 5 to 30 minutes if the reduction succeeds.

quiz.q: A 52-year-old with four days of low back pain reports numbness between his legs and says he has not urinated since yesterday. What is the priority?
choices: NSAIDs and early mobilization advice
Urgent evaluation for cauda equina syndrome with emergent MRI
Bladder scan, then outpatient urology referral
Lumbar radiographs and discharge
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia with urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise, and delay causes permanent incontinence. Plain films will not show it and outpatient referral loses the window for surgery.

scenarios.title: Dog bite to the hand with a tendon concern
scenarios.intro: `21:15`. A `34-year-old` mail carrier is triaged with a dog bite to the right hand, sustained about `90 minutes` ago while delivering to a house with a loose German shepherd. He is right-handed. There is a ragged tear across the back of the hand near the base of the index finger and two puncture marks on the palm side. He is holding the hand wrapped in a towel and has not looked at it since it happened.

steps.prompt:
You are getting him into a room. Bleeding has stopped. He wants to know how many stitches he needs.

**What do you do before anything is cleaned or numbed?**

choices.text: Document tendon function, nerve function and perfusion in the hand, and ask about the dog, the tetanus history and his occupation
choices.feedback: Correct. Once the hand is anesthetized nobody can demonstrate what was working beforehand. The dog's status drives the rabies decision, tetanus drives the vaccine decision, and being a right-handed mail carrier changes what a missed tendon costs him.

choices.text: Irrigate immediately, since early irrigation lowers infection rates
choices.feedback: Irrigation matters enormously and is coming. But a functional exam recorded before the anesthetic is the one thing that cannot be recovered afterward, and it takes ninety seconds.

choices.text: Get an x-ray first to look for a retained tooth
choices.feedback: Reasonable for a bite over a joint and it will likely happen. It is not the first step, and it does not substitute for a documented tendon and nerve exam.

choices.text: Tell him it looks like about six stitches and take him for registration
choices.feedback: Most hand bites are not closed at all, so the answer is probably zero. More importantly, nothing has been examined yet, and a promise about closure sets an expectation the physician will have to undo.

steps.prompt:
You examine the hand. He can make a fist, but when you hold the middle joint of the index finger straight and ask him to bend the fingertip, it moves — weakly, and it hurts. Extension of the index finger against your resistance is clearly weaker than the left. Sensation is intact everywhere and capillary refill is brisk.

**How do you interpret and report this?**

choices.text: Full range of motion means the tendons are intact; report it as a soft tissue injury
choices.feedback: This is the most common and most consequential error in hand wounds. A partially cut tendon still moves — it just moves weakly. Full motion never excludes a tendon injury.

choices.text: Report a possible partial tendon injury: weak but present FDP flexion and weak extension against resistance, with intact sensation and perfusion
choices.feedback: Correct, and the phrasing matters. Naming which tendon, which test and what you compared it to gives the physician something to act on and gives hand surgery something to triage.

choices.text: Report that the weakness is probably from pain and recheck after analgesia
choices.feedback: Pain does reduce effort, which is why the finding is reported rather than dismissed. Attributing weakness to pain is how a partial tendon laceration goes home and ruptures completely four days later.

choices.text: Report weakness in the index finger and ask the physician to examine the hand before anything is numbed
choices.feedback: Correct and appropriately humble. Escalating an abnormal finding before the anesthetic goes in is exactly right, even without naming the specific tendon.

steps.prompt:
The physician confirms your findings and orders an x-ray of the hand, irrigation, tetanus, and antibiotics. His last tetanus shot was "maybe eight years ago, when I stepped on something." The dog is the homeowner's, currently confined, up to date on vaccines, and animal control has it.

**What does he need for tetanus and rabies?**

choices.text: Tetanus vaccine now; observe the dog for 10 days with no rabies prophylaxis
choices.feedback: Correct on both. A bite wound is not clean and minor, so the interval is 5 years, and eight exceeds it. A healthy, available, confined dog is observed for 10 days, and prophylaxis begins only if it develops signs.

choices.text: No tetanus needed at 8 years; observe the dog 10 days
choices.feedback: The rabies half is right. The tetanus half uses the wrong interval — 10 years applies only to clean minor wounds, and any other wound uses 5 years. This is the single most commonly missed number in wound care.

choices.text: Tetanus vaccine plus immune globulin, and start the full rabies series now
choices.feedback: Both are over-treatment. Immune globulin is added only for fewer than three lifetime doses or an unknown history, and rabies prophylaxis is not started when a healthy dog is available for the 10-day observation.

choices.text: Tetanus vaccine now, and start rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3
choices.feedback: Tetanus is right. The days 0 and 3 schedule is the abbreviated course for someone already vaccinated against rabies, and none of it is indicated while the dog is under observation.

steps.prompt:
The x-ray shows no fracture and no radiopaque fragment. You irrigate copiously with saline. The physician says the wounds are to be left open, dressed, splinted, and the patient is going to hand surgery in the morning.

**The patient asks why you are not sewing it up. What is the honest answer?**

choices.text: "We're short-staffed tonight, so hand surgery will close it tomorrow."
choices.feedback: Untrue and it undermines the plan. He will interpret an open wound as neglect and may not come back tomorrow. The reason is medical, and it is easy to explain.

choices.text: "Closing a bite traps bacteria inside. Hand bites infect badly, so we clean them, leave them open, and cover you with antibiotics while the tendon gets checked properly."
choices.feedback: Correct, plain, and true. Patients accept an open wound readily once they understand that closing it would seal the infection in. Naming the tendon concern also explains why hand surgery is involved at all.

choices.text: "Bites are never closed, ever."
choices.feedback: Close, but overstated. Facial bites are often closed after thorough irrigation for cosmetic reasons. Hand, cat, human and late-presenting bites are the ones left open, and this is a hand bite.

choices.text: "It's too small to need stitches."
choices.feedback: Wrong reason, and it minimizes an injury that may involve a tendon. He will conclude the whole thing is trivial and skip the morning appointment.

steps.prompt:
You are applying a splint and giving discharge instructions for the overnight period. He is on amoxicillin-clavulanate and has an `08:00` hand surgery appointment.

**What must the instructions include?**

choices.text: Keep it dry and elevated, take the antibiotic, and come back for the appointment
choices.feedback: The basics are there but the safety net is not. A hand bite can develop a spreading infection overnight, and he needs to know which specific changes mean coming back before `08:00`.

choices.text: Elevate above the heart, keep the splint dry, complete the antibiotic, keep the 08:00 appointment, and return immediately for increasing pain, spreading redness, red streaks, fever, drainage, numbness or inability to move the fingers
choices.feedback: Correct. The return precautions are the point: a hand infection or a compartment problem declares itself in hours, and he is going home before the swelling peaks. Write them down as well as saying them.

choices.text: Elevate, keep dry, and soak the hand in warm water three times overnight to draw out infection
choices.feedback: Soaking macerates the wound edges, wets the splint, and does not draw anything out. Elevation and antibiotics are the treatment.

choices.text: Splint the hand flat so it stays comfortable overnight
choices.feedback: A hand splinted flat stiffens. The position of safety is the wrist extended 20 to 30 degrees, knuckles bent 70 to 90, and the finger joints nearly straight.

scenarios.debrief:
Three things nearly went wrong in this case, and all three are tech-level catches.

**Full motion is not an intact tendon.** He made a fist. He also had measurably weak flexion and extension on the injured side, which is exactly what a partial laceration produces. Strength against resistance, compared with the other hand, is the test — and it has to be done and written down **before** the anesthetic.

**Bites are not closed.** The instinct to fix what is torn is strong, and closing a hand bite converts an open contaminated wound into a sealed abscess over a tendon sheath. Cephalexin would have been the other version of the same error, because it does not cover `Pasteurella`.

**The five-year tetanus interval.** Eight years sounded fine to him and would have sounded fine to most people. Any wound that is not clean and minor uses `5 years`, not `10`.

And the rabies decision was made on the **animal**, not the wound: a healthy, confined, available dog gets observed for `10 days` while nothing is given.

scenarios.title: Fall onto an outstretched hand
scenarios.intro: `10:40`. A `68-year-old` woman slipped on wet leaves on her front steps and landed on her right hand with the wrist bent back. She is in triage holding her forearm against her body. There is an obvious bump on the back of the wrist. She takes a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis and lives alone in a two-storey house.

steps.prompt:
You bring her to a room. The wrist has a visible step-off on the back, with swelling from the knuckles to mid-forearm.

**What is the exam you perform and record?**

choices.text: Look, feel and check motion, plus radial pulse, capillary refill, and median, ulnar and radial sensation and motor function — then check the elbow and shoulder too
choices.feedback: Correct. Distal neurovascular status before anything is splinted or moved, and the joint above and below because the force that broke the wrist travelled up the arm. The median nerve is the one at risk here.

choices.text: Check the radial pulse and get her to x-ray quickly, since the deformity is obvious
choices.feedback: A pulse is not a neurovascular exam. Median nerve compression from a displaced distal radius fracture is common, and a deficit found after the splint with no baseline is an unanswerable question.

choices.text: Splint it in a position of comfort first, then examine once the pain settles
choices.feedback: Splinting before the exam is backwards. Once the splint is on, the exam has to be repeated anyway, and any deficit discovered afterward cannot be separated from the splinting.

choices.text: Examine the wrist thoroughly; the elbow and shoulder are not involved in a wrist injury
choices.feedback: The wrist exam is right, but the rule for any limb injury is the joint above and below. A fall on an outstretched hand transmits force through the forearm, elbow and shoulder, and elderly patients localize poorly.

steps.prompt:
Pulse and refill are normal. Sensation is intact but she reports "pins and needles" in the thumb, index and middle fingers that started in the ambulance. She can still make an `OK` sign, weakly. Elbow and shoulder are non-tender.

**What does the tingling mean, and what do you do with it?**

choices.text: Normal after a fall; note it and continue
choices.feedback: The thumb, index and middle finger distribution is the median nerve, and new symptoms there after a displaced distal radius fracture suggest acute carpal tunnel compression. It is escalated, not noted in passing.

choices.text: Median nerve symptoms from the displaced fracture — report it to the physician now and record the exact time it started
choices.feedback: Correct. Acute median nerve compression can change this from a next-week reduction to a same-hour one. The onset time matters because it defines how long the nerve has been compressed.

choices.text: Ulnar nerve compression; pad the inner elbow
choices.feedback: Wrong nerve. The ulnar nerve serves the little finger and half the ring finger. Thumb, index and middle is median territory, which runs through the carpal tunnel right at the fracture.

choices.text: Anxiety-related hyperventilation causing tingling
choices.feedback: Hyperventilation tingling is bilateral and involves the lips and both hands. A single-limb, single-nerve distribution next to a fracture is a nerve, not a breathing pattern.

steps.prompt:
The physician evaluates her and orders wrist films. The x-ray shows a distal radius fracture, extra-articular, dorsally displaced and angulated, with an associated ulnar styloid fracture. No scaphoid fracture is seen.

**What is this pattern called, and is anything still unresolved on the imaging?**

choices.text: A Smith fracture; nothing further is needed
choices.feedback: A Smith fracture is displaced toward the palm, from a fall on a flexed wrist. Dorsal displacement after a fall on an extended wrist is a Colles fracture.

choices.text: A Colles fracture — and her snuffbox should be palpated, because scaphoid fractures are often invisible on the first films
choices.feedback: Correct on both. Dorsal displacement with a dinner-fork deformity after a fall on an outstretched hand is a Colles fracture. The same mechanism causes scaphoid fractures, and a negative first x-ray does not exclude one.

choices.text: A Colles fracture; the negative scaphoid view rules out any carpal injury
choices.feedback: The name is right but the conclusion is not. Scaphoid fractures are frequently invisible for 10 to 14 days, so the exam — snuffbox tenderness — overrides the film.

choices.text: A Galeazzi fracture, because the ulna is involved
choices.feedback: Galeazzi is a distal radius fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint, not simply an ulnar styloid chip. This is a Colles fracture with an ulnar styloid avulsion, which is a common companion.

steps.prompt:
A reduction under procedural sedation is planned in the room. You are setting up and assisting.

**What is your sequence?**

choices.text: Monitor, pulse oximetry, capnography, oxygen, suction, bag-valve mask, airway equipment and reversal agents at the bedside; neurovascular exam documented again immediately before; then countertraction as directed; then post-reduction film; then recheck the nerve exam; then splint
choices.feedback: Correct and in the right order. Sedation setup first because that is what can kill her, documentation immediately before because the reduction itself can injure the nerve, and the recheck afterward because that is the comparison that matters.

choices.text: Apply the splint first so it is ready, then sedate and reduce through it
choices.feedback: The splint is moulded to hold the reduced position, so it goes on after. Reducing through a splint is neither possible nor safe.

choices.text: Set up monitoring and oxygen, assist with the reduction, then splint and discharge her once she is awake
choices.feedback: The monitoring half is right, but capnography, suction, airway equipment and reversal agents belong at the bedside for any procedural sedation, and the post-reduction film and nerve recheck cannot be skipped.

choices.text: Get the post-reduction film after the splint is applied and dried, for a cleaner picture
choices.feedback: Films are obtained before the splint hardens in most departments precisely so an inadequate reduction can be corrected immediately rather than re-done an hour later. Sequence varies by protocol, but waiting for plaster to dry is not the reason.

steps.prompt:
The reduction is good on the post-reduction film. A sugar-tong splint is on. Her tingling has already improved. She is awake, alert and asking when she can drive. She lives alone, upstairs bedroom, no family in the state.

**What does her discharge need to cover?**

choices.text: Orthopedic follow-up in a week, pain medication, and instructions to keep the splint dry
choices.feedback: The essentials of the fracture are covered, but nothing here addresses the swelling window, the return precautions, or the fact that she is going back to an empty two-storey house with one usable arm.

choices.text: Elevate above the heart for 48 to 72 hours, ice over the splint, keep it dry, nothing pushed inside it, orthopedic follow-up within a week, and explicit return precautions for increasing pain, numbness, or pale, blue, cold or immobile fingers — plus a plan for how she manages at home alone
choices.feedback: Correct. The return precautions are a compartment syndrome screen handed to the patient, because she goes home before the swelling peaks. And a 68-year-old alone in a two-storey house with one arm is a fall risk and a social-work or case-management conversation, not just an ortho one.

choices.text: Tell her to remove the splint if it feels too tight and reapply it loosely
choices.feedback: She must never adjust the splint herself — it is holding a reduction. A splint that feels too tight is a reason to come back, and that distinction has to be said clearly.

choices.text: Advise her to keep the arm dependent at her side so blood flow to the fingers is maintained
choices.feedback: This is backwards for the first few days. Elevation above the heart reduces the swelling that causes the complications. Keeping a limb at heart level rather than elevated applies specifically to suspected compartment syndrome, not to routine post-splint care.

scenarios.debrief:
A fall onto an outstretched hand is the most common mechanism in the department, and it produces four injuries worth knowing by name: **Colles** at the distal radius, **scaphoid** in the carpus, **radial head** at the elbow, and **proximal humerus** at the shoulder. The reason you examine the joint above and below is that the same fall produces all of them, and an older patient will only tell you about the one that hurts most.

The finding that changed the tempo was **new tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers**. That distribution is the median nerve, running through the carpal tunnel directly under a dorsally displaced fracture, and reporting it with a start time is what turns a routine reduction into a prompt one.

The negative scaphoid view proved nothing. **Snuffbox tenderness with a normal film is a scaphoid fracture until repeat imaging says otherwise**, because the blood supply runs backward up the bone and a missed proximal fracture dies.

And the last step was not orthopedic at all. She is `68`, alone, upstairs, with one working arm. That is a return visit waiting to happen, and naming it is part of the discharge.
